Abstract
A rheological model for loose granular media is developed to capture both solid-like and fluid-like responses during shear­
ing. The proposed model is built by following the mathematical structure of an extended Kelvin–Voigt model, where an 
elastic spring and plastic slider act in parallel to a viscous damper. This arrangement requires the partition of the total 
stress into rate-independent and rate-dependent stress components. To model the solid-like behavior, a simple frictional 
plasticity model is adopted without modifications, thus contributing to the rate-independent stress. Instead, the fluid-like 
or rate-dependent stress is further decomposed into deviatoric and volumetric parts, by proposing a new formulation based 
on a combination of the µ(I) relation, originally developed under pressure-controlled shear, with a pressure-shear rate 
relation derived under volume-controlled shear. The proposed formulation allows the model to capture both the increase 
in the friction coefficient and the enhanced dilation at high shear rates. High-fidelity simulation data, obtained from dis­
crete element method and multiscale modelling, are used to evaluate the performance of the proposed constitutive model. 
The model provides accurate results under both drained and undrained simple shear paths across a wide range of shear 
rates. Furthermore, it successfully reproduces at much lower computational cost the flowslide mobility computed through 
multiscale simulations, which is primarily regulated by the shear rate dependence of the material properties during the 
dynamic runout stage.

and ϕJ( Jamming point) [32]. Within this range, the granu­

but may exhibit fluid-like behavior under external loading, 
where particles remain closely packed and interact through 
both collision and long-lived contacts [3]. Based on the con­
tinuum description of water-saturated granular assemblies 
within this ϕ range [e.g., 7, 11], the effective granular stress 
associated with the granular skeleton plays a critical role 
in the motion of the solid phase, alongside water-particle 
interactions such as inter-phase viscous drag and buoyancy. 
This stress, corresponding to the Terzaghi effective stress, 
governs the solid phase’s response. This study focuses on 
describing the solid- and fluid-like components within the 
effective stress, as they are broadly associated with the 
triggering and post-failure responses of a flowslide event, 
respectively.
Numerous advanced plasticity models have been devel­
oped to replicate the solid-like behaviors exhibited by 
granular materials, including Nor-sand [23], MIT-S1 [37], 
and SANISAND [16, 44, 53], to name a few. Modeling the 
solid-like response of soils, including contraction/dilation, 
strain localization, and the critical state, remains a central 
and fascinating topic in the soil mechanics community. 
In contrast, modeling the fluid-like response of granular 
materials focuses primarily on post-yield or post-failure 
rate-dependent behaviors, where the key challenge lies in 
the formulation of the viscosity term. Rheological models 
based on µ(I) rheology or kinetic theory have been used 
extensively for granular flow applications [e.g., 21, 24, 5, 
51, 9]. However, in the case of dense granular flow, many 
studies adopt a simplified version of µ(I) rheology by dis­
regarding the associated Φ(I) relation (i.e., the volume 
change induced by high shear rates),  also referred to as 
incompressible µ(I) rheology [e.g., 5]. While this simplifi­
cation may be reasonable for dry granular flows where vol­
ume effects on the shear response are negligible, it can lead 
to significant discrepancies when granular media are fluid-
saturated, thus rendering transient pore fluid flow invariably 
coupled with volume changes. Under such conditions, it 
becomes imperative to consider the influence of shear rate 
on the dilative tendencies of granular media, which will in 
turn affect the shear response. To address this, a few stud­
ies  [6, 42] have developed the compressible I-dependent 
rheology (CIDR) framework, where a dilatancy function is 
formulated in terms of strain rate by inverting the Φ(I) rela­
tion. Following this approach, Bagnold’s law (p ∝˙γ2) is 
attained. However, Bagnold’s law is not universal; it is pri­
marily valid for loose granular assemblies under small shear 
rates, as confirmed by DEM simulations of constant-vol­
ume (undrained) simple shear tests [14, 45]. This limitation 
likely arises because the µ(I) rheology is developed based 
on pressure-controlled (constant vertical normal stress, or 
drained) simple shear tests, which may inadequately repre­
sent responses under constant-volume conditions. An attrac­
tive alternative is given by rheological model specifically 
designed to cope with constant-volume conditions, which 
aims at linking shear rate and steady state pressure [14, 45]. 
More recently, efforts have been made to extend the CIDR 
framework by incorporating such links [43], but the model’s 
performance still requires further evaluation. To the authors’ 
knowledge, a fluid-like model that seamlessly integrates 
both pressure-controlled and volume-controlled rheologies, 
while demonstrating robust performance, remains an open 
challenge.
Despite this challenge, numerous efforts have been made 
towards unified models that encompass both the solid- and 
fluid-like response of granular media [e.g., 2, 17, 19, 46, 1, 
34, 9]. These models generally start from the combination

This paper aims to address a specific aspect of the rate-
dependent behavior that has so far received limited attention: 
the formulation of an effective volume-controlled rheology. 
Employing the extended Kelvin–Voigt structure, the pro­
posed model integrates a simple frictional plasticity model 
for the solid-like component. The fluid-like component is 
carefully formulated to align with the solid-like component, 
so that the proposed model can properly capture both tran­
sient and steady-state behaviors of granular materials under 
varying shear rates. The performance of the proposed model 
is assessed through simulations using high-fidelity numeri­
cal data obtained from both discrete element method (DEM) 
and multiscale modeling. The stress decomposition in the 
extended Kelvin–Voigt model may evoke comparisons to 
the decomposition of the homogenized stress in particle 
assemblies, which accounts for contributions from contact 
forces or particle fluctuating velocities [e.g., 10, 48]. How­

solid- and fluid-like components are assumed to originate 
from contact forces between particles, aligning with the 
“effective stress” concept in soil mechanics. The kinetic

included in this study, as its contribution has been shown 
to be negligible by [33, 50, 52]. Specifically, the solid-like 
component represents the response of the granular assem­
bly under quasi-static loading conditions, where the fluid-
like contribution is negligible (creep is not considered in 
this study). Under dynamic loading, the fluid-like compo­
nent emerges as the difference between the total dynamic 
response and the quasi-static response. While this assump­
tion may warrant further scrutiny, it provides a straightfor­
ward and practical approach for the current study.

In soil mechanics, drained (or pressured-controlled) 
and undrained (or volume-controlled) simple shear tests 
typically refer to controlling the flow of water in a water-
saturated soil sample by either opening or closing a valve, 
allowing or preventing water from flowing out of the sample 
during shearing. In this process, a constant vertical stress 
is applied to the top of the sample, which is the effective 
stress in drained tests and the total stress in undrained tests. 
In constitutive modeling, a drained simple shear test is 
characterized by maintaining a constant vertical effective 
stress (or pressure-controlled condition), which allows the 
sample to contract or dilate during shearing. This concept 
also applies to typical DEM simulations where only dry 
particles are considered. The undrained simple shear test is 
simulated by preserving the sample’s volume, often referred 
to as constant-volume simple shear test, due to the signifi­
cant difference in the bulk modulus between water and the 
solid skeleton. The vertical stress computed in constant-
volume tests is the effective stress, and any reduction in this 
stress from its initial value corresponds to the excess pore 
pressure.
2  Model development
For simplicity, this study demonstrates the development of 
the rheological model in the simple shear stress space, where 
shear stress τ and normal stress σ represent the deviatoric 
and volumetric components, respectively. The correspond­
ing multi-axial formulations based on the full stress tensor 
σ can be derived by referring to studies such as [24]. The 
standard sign convention in soil mechanics is used, where 
compressive stress is considered positive.
2.1  Reference solid-state model
To accurately model the solid–fluid transition, it is crucial 
for the reference model to effectively capture key character­
istics of loose sands. These include frictional failure under 
drained conditions and liquefaction-type failure promoted 
by undrained or partially drained conditions. These features 
play a significant role in triggering a flowslide event. Sev­
eral sand models serve this purpose, such as Nor-sand [23], 
MIT-S1 [37], and SANISAND [16], among others. How­
ever, these models are not chosen in this study. The ratio­
nale behind this decision is that they are based on critical 
state theory (CST) developed under quasi-static loading, 
and extending this theory to dynamic loading conditions 
presents significant challenges. For example, CST and 
µ(I) rheology are inherently incompatible. At critical state,

2.3  Steady state conditions
Proposing appropriate expressions for ζ in Eq. (7) and η in 
Eq. (10) to adequately capture the transient response of the 
granular system is challenging. Hence, a more convenient 
approach is to leverage the established knowledge of the

4  Model performance
To evaluate the performance of the proposed model in simu­
lating the response of granular materials under various shear 
rates, we require the corresponding laboratory experimental 
data. While there is abundant experimental data concern­
ing the quasi-static response of sands, data considering the 
rate effect is relatively scarce. To overcome this limitation, 
an integrated virtual testing strategy relying on both DEM 
and multiscale modelling is adopted hereafter. DEM is 
employed to conduct drained and undrained simple shear 
tests across a range of strain rates, while multiscale model­
ing, originally developed to examine the effect of strain rate 
on flowslide triggering and runout [52], is used to gener­
ate data with varying strain rates along the shear process. 
These simulated data enable us to assess the capability of 
the proposed constitutive model in capturing the rheological 
response of granular materials across different shear rates. 
The details of the setup for DEM simulations are presented 
in Appendix A.

A multiscale modeling framework, coupling a continuum 
model with a local solver based on DEM, has recently been 
established to investigate the influence of strain rate on 
flowslide triggering and runout [52]. The continuum model, 
referred to as the sliding consolidation model (SCM) [12], 
solves the equations of linear momentum balance and fluid 
diffusion, where a constitutive model for sands is required 
for completeness. Instead of relying on a traditional con­
stitutive model, a DEM sample is incorporated into SCM 
to simulate the material behavior, to achieve the multiscale 
modeling. Figure 10 provides a schematic of this hierarchi­
cal multiscale modelling framework, where SCM trans­

accordingly and returns stress information to SCM. In this 
framework, two types of information passing are proposed: 
rate-independent (RI) and rate-dependent (RD) DEMs. 
The key distinction lies their handling of strain rates. For a 
given strain increment passed from SCM, RI-DEM always 
deforms at a quasi-static strain rate, regardless of the strain 
rate from SCM. In contrast, RD-DEM respects and respond 
to the strain rate from SCM. When analyzing a flowslide 
event, comparing results from SCM+RI-DEM and SCM-

triggering and runout. For instance, Yang and Buscarnera 
[52] demonstrated that the dynamics of flowslide runout in 
loose sands depend on two macroscale effects regulated by 
the shear rate: (i) the increased friction coefficient and (ii) 
the enhanced dilation. In this study, simulation data from 
the multiscale modeling framework are used to evaluate 
whether the proposed constitutive model can effectively 
capture these two aforementioned effects.

5  Conclusion
This paper develops a rheological model to unify the simu­
lation of both solid-like and fluid-like behaviors of loose 
granular media, based on the mathematical structure of the 
extended Kelvin–Voigt model. A simple frictional plasticity 
model [36] that can capture essential features of loose sands 
is adopted as the reference solid-state model; mathematical 
expressions that account for the µ(I) relation under pres­
sure-controlled shear  [24] and a pressure-shear rate rela­
tion under volume-controlled shear [14] are formulated to 
constitute the fluid-like component, without modifying the 
reference model.
The proposed model performance in simulating the rate 
effects of granular flow is evaluated using data from DEM 
and multiscale simulations. The proposed model effectively 
reproduces the µ(I) rheology and the pressure-shear rate 
relation in drained and undrained simple shear tests, respec­
tively, despite some discrepancies in capturing the transient 
response during the early stage of shearing. Furthermore, 
the proposed model is integrated into a SCM framework for 
unified simulation of flowslide triggering and runout. The 
proposed model accurately captures the flowslide mobil­
ity observed in the multiscale simulation using SCM+RD-
DEM, including both the transient and steady-state 
responses, by essentially reflecting (i) the increased friction 
coefficient and (ii) the enhanced dilation due to high shear 
rates.
There are potential enhancements for the rheological 
model proposed in this study. These include addressing the 
out-of-sync evolution of fluid-like shear stress and kinetic 
pressure, and integrating the critical state theory [e.g., 39]. 
Despite its current limitations, the use of this model in a very 
challenging setting, involving partial drainage, dynamics, 
and seamless transition from quasi-static trigger to dynamic 
runout emphasizes the benefits of the proposed approach 
and encourages its verification against measurements and 
its further development.

The DEM simulations referenced in Sects.  2.4, 4.1, 
and  4.2 are performed using the open-source DEM pro­
gram LIGGGHTS [26]. The granular assembly consists of 
polydisperse spherical particles that interact through soft-
particle laws, specially a Hertzian normal model and a his­
tory-dependent tangential model with a Coulomb friction 
cut-off. Detailed descriptions of these contact models can be 
found in the LIGGGHTS documentation. The DEM param­
eters, including particle density ρ, Young’s modulus E, Pois­
son’s ratio ν, coefficient of restitution ϵ, tangential friction 
coefficient µ, are summarized in Table 2. The rationale for 
selecting these parameter is thoroughly discussed in [52].
In this study, DEM samples are generated using 3400 
spheres with two diameter sizes: 2e-3 m and 2.4e-3 m, 
each containing the same mass. The particles are randomly 
inserted into a large three-dimensional periodic cell to avoid 
any initial overlaps. The sample is then subjected to iso­
tropic compression to achieve the target stress state, using 
a servo-control algorithm to govern the motion of the cell 
boundaries. The compression process consists of two main 
substeps: (1) the tangential friction coefficient µ is set to 
0.48 to prepare a loose packing. Isotropic compression is 
applied until the sample reaches 10% of the target pressure. 
(2) the top and bottom periodic boundaries are expanded, 
and a layer of particles is formed to act as a wall, facilitat­
ing the subsequent shearing process. The lateral boundar­
ies remain periodic (bi-periodic), and isotropic compression 
is resumed with µ = 0.5 until the target stress state is 
achieved. The target pressure in this study is 28.4 kPa and 
the prepared sample has a volume fraction of 0.5839. Fig­
ure 14a displays the sample prepared using this procedure.

Abstract: A rheological model for loose granular media is developed to capture both solid-like and fluid-like responses during shear­ ing. The proposed model is built by following the mathematical structure of an extended Kelvin–Voigt model, where an elastic spring and plastic slider act in parallel to a viscous damper. This arrangement requires the partition of the total stress into rate-independent and rate-dependent stress components. To model the solid-like behavior, a simple frictional plasticity model is adopted without modifications, thus contributing to the rate-independent stress. Instead, the fluid-like or rate-dependent stress is further decomposed into deviatoric and volumetric parts, by proposing a new formulation based on a combination of the µ(I) relation, originally developed under pressure-controlled shear, with a pressure-shear rate relation derived under volume-controlled shear. The proposed formulation allows the model to capture both the increase in the friction coefficient and the enhanced dilation at high shear rates. High-fidelity simulation data, obtained from dis­ crete element method and multiscale modelling, are used to evaluate the performance of the proposed constitutive model. The model provides accurate results under both drained and undrained simple shear paths across a wide range of shear rates. Furthermore, it successfully reproduces at much lower computational cost the flowslide mobility computed through multiscale simulations, which is primarily regulated by the shear rate dependence of the material properties during the dynamic runout stage.
